## **1.0 Introduction**

Although avian and bat mortalities caused by collisions with wind turbines have been well documented in a number of study reports, the impacts of new facilities on avian and bat populations often are not fully known until operations begin.  Many companies now conduct post-construction studies to evaluate how their turbines affect bird and bat populations.  In this study, Buffalo Gap Wind Farm 2, LLC (BG2) contracted with TRC to conduct an avian mortality study of the newly operational Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm facility in Nolan County, Texas.  The purpose of this study was to estimate the impacts of the wind farm on birds and bats and to determine if the standardized sampling protocols of Erickson et al. (2000) are appropriate for detecting mortality in bats and in smaller birds such as the black-capped vireo ( _Vireo atricapillus_ ), a federal and state endangered species that is known to occur in the oak-juniper woodlands of Nolan County.

This 14-month study began in July 2007, was suspended in May 2008 due to budget constraints, then resumed in September 2008, and ended in December 2008.  Nine searcher accuracy trials and nine scavenger removal trials ( _sensu_ Erickson et al. 2000) were incorporated into the study to more accurately estimate the wind farm related mortality based on the total number of carcasses found during the study.

The Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm is located approximately 38 km (24 mi) southwest of Abilene, Texas. Construction of the facility was completed in late 2005 and the 155 1.5-megawatt (MW) wind turbines began operation in June 2007.  The wind farm is situated on an east-west oriented bluff that is part of the Callahan Divide (Texas State Historical Association 1999). Most of the turbines at the Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm are arranged along the north and south edges of the bluff.  Winds in the Buffalo Gap and Abilene areas are predominantly from the south and southeast (Natural Resources Conservation Service 2001).  The area is mostly dominated by dense thickets of ashe juniper ( _Juniperus ashei_ ), post oak ( _Quercus stellata_ ), and mesquite ( _Prosopsis glandulosa_ ) with smaller inclusions of grassland and dryland agricultural fields.  Major land uses in the area include livestock grazing, commercial hunting, agriculture, and energy production.  Average elevation on the wind farm is about 758 m (2,487 ft).

A subset of 36 turbines was selected from the array of 155 turbines now operating on-site (Appendix A). This subset of turbines was selected as a representative sample of the project area’s varied landforms and terrain, different portions of the turbine strings, variations in vegetative cover, and other physical features found throughout the area.  The criteria for selecting the turbines included: proximity to cliff faces and waters such as intermittent streams, proximity to the edges of the turbine array and open fields, appropriate habitat for bats and the black-capped vireo, and proximity to other turbines or man-made features such as substations, power lines, and roads.

Turbines 80, 93, 100, 115, 120 146, 167, 171, 175, 190, 193, 196, and 216 are located on an elongated elevated plateau that runs through the middle of the project area (Appendix A), while Turbine 83 is located on Indian Head Bluff at the south west end of the project area.  Turbines 124, 128, 130, 151, 158, 177 and 185 are located north of Birdsnest Bluff at the west end of the project area.  Turbine 209 is located near Robtann Draw.  Turbines 201 and 221 are located south of Ranch Road 2035 in the northwest corner of the project area.  Turbines 68, 85, 90, and 106 are located north of Mulberry Canyon in the southeast corner of the project area.  Turbines 132 and 134 are located west of Mulberry Canyon in close proximity of Ringtop, near the east boundary of the project area.  Turbines 143 and 160 are situated on a rise overlooking Coffee Hollow.  Turbines 188, 211, 213, and 215 are located south of Ranch Road 2035 near Weaver Springs Creek in the northeast quarter of the project area.

## **2.0 Survey Methods**

## **2.1 Carcass Searches**

The purpose of this study was to estimate the impacts of the Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm on bird and bat species and to determine if the standardized sampling protocols of Erickson et al. (2000) were sensitive enough to detect mortality in bats and in smaller birds such as the black-capped vireo, a federal and state endangered species that may occur in the project area’s oak-juniper woodlands.

Carcass searches were conducted at 36 turbines during the 14-month study period from July 2007 through May 2008 (total of 10 months).  The study was suspended at the request of BG2 due to budget constraints, and resumed in September through December 2008 (total of 4 months). All avian and bat carcasses, as well as feather spots observed within the study plots, were recorded and, where possible, a cause of death was determined. The number of avian and bat fatalities attributable to collisions with the wind turbines or towers was estimated based on the number of carcasses and feather spots found and searcher accuracy and scavenger bias results. The sampling protocol follows that developed by Erickson and Hazelwood (2004) for the Judith Gap, Montana project and is similar to the standardized monitoring protocols reported by Erickson et al. (2000); Erickson et al. (2003a) and (2003b); and Young et al. (2003).

Erickson and Hazelwood (2004) have shown that nearly all fatalities are found within the distance from the turbine equal to the turbine tip height, as measured from the base of the turbine, with a large majority of the carcasses found within a distance equal to 50% of the base to tip height.  Data collected by Orloff and Flannery (1992), Higgins et al. (1996), and Johnson et al. (2002), also suggests that the most birds and bats killed by striking turbine blades or towers remain within 63 m of the turbine.  Since the turbine tip height for this project is 118 m (387.1 ft) and the terrain in much of the project area is rugged, 244 x 244 m (800 x 800 ft) rectangular plots were laid out and centered on each turbine.  Using this size of study plot, however, resulted in some overlap among study plots so the plot size was adjusted to 215 x 215 m (705 x 705 ft).

Thirty-one belt transects were laid out approximately 6 m (20 ft) apart within each study plot. The transect routes were also downloaded into handheld global positioning system (GPS) units and used to indicate the surveyor's direction and position relative to the turbine, previously collected data points, and the boundaries of the study plot (Appendix B).  Each survey began at the southeast corner of the transect grid and a digital photograph was taken from this corner facing northwest toward the turbine (Appendix C).  Approximately 7.0 km (4.4 mi) of transect were traversed in each study plot and 4.60 ha (11.4 acres) surrounding each turbine were surveyed for avian and bat casualties every 2 to 3 weeks.

Qualified biologists trained in the search techniques conducted the searches. On average, 3.5 hours were spent searching each turbine (Appendix D). The species, sex, and age (when possible); date and time observed; location; condition; and comments related to time of and probable cause of death were recorded for each casualty (Appendix D).  The condition of each casualty found and recorded as a strike was assessed using the following condition classes:  Intact-a carcass that is completely intact, is not badly decomposed, and shows little or no sign of being fed upon by a predator or scavenger; Scavengedremains of a carcass showing signs of being fed upon, scavenged, or dismembered with scattered remains; Feather Spot-ten or more feathers at one location indicating decomposition or scavenging. Feather spots consisting of two or more primary feathers also were counted as strikes unless their position, age, or condition indicated that they were part of previously recorded remains or that they pre-dated the on-line date of the wind project (June 2007).

Fatalities found in non-search areas were treated as incidental discoveries and consequently were not included in the estimation of facility-related fatalities.  However, the locations of all carcasses were

recorded with GPS using the Universal Transverse Mercator UTM) coordinate system (Appendix D) and the carcasses were marked with silver glitter, photographed (Appendix C), and revisited in subsequent monthly sampling events in order to determine the rate of scavenging.

Collection of state and federal endangered, threatened, or protected species did not occur in this study and further coordination with the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) was not required.  Prior to initiation of the study, however, the Buffalo Gap wind farm personnel were provided with instructions on how to document carcass finds.  Fatalities found by those not conducting the formal searches within 215 m (705 ft) of monitored wind turbines, were documented with photographs and the data were included in a wildlife incident report.  Fatalities found in non-search areas were treated as incidental discoveries and consequently were not included in the final fatality total.

## **2.2 Carcass Search Biases**

## **2.2.1 Searcher Accuracy**

The objective of this portion of the study was to determine the searchers’ ability and accuracy in detecting randomly placed models within the study plots.  Searcher accuracy trials were conducted in the same areas that the carcass searches occurred.  Detection of randomly placed models within the study plots was evaluated using three size classes of papier-maché and hunting decoys as models representing small, medium, and large birds.  Estimated searcher accuracy was then used in conjunction with the total number of carcasses found to adjust the fatality estimate for detection bias.

Sixty-nine models representing small, medium, and large birds were distributed throughout the study plots during each of nine bi-weekly sampling events in August 2007, October 2007, February 2008, March 2008, April 2008, May 2008, October 2008, November 2008, and December 2008.  Twenty-seven small bird models representing represented the warblers, and vireos, 27 medium models representing birds such as quail, and 15 large hunting decoys or models representing raptors and turkey vultures were placed at different turbines.  Models were marked with an identification number and the trial date.  The models were distributed at random locations within the turbine plots in the morning of the same day or the day prior to scheduled turbine searches, and the locations were recorded by the calibrator responsible for distributing the models within the project area.

Individuals conducting the carcass searches did not know when or where these calibration trials would be conducted. When models were found, the searcher recorded its identification number, location, and the date that it was placed in the project area.  All remaining models were recorded when found. GPS data points were taken by both the calibrator and the searcher for comparison, to identify models if the model number was damaged, and to check on the status of models not found. The searcher accuracy rate was averaged across the three model sizes and the nine sample dates.

## **2.2.2 Scavenging Removal Trials**

Estimates of carcass removal by scavengers were used to adjust carcass counts and to estimate the length of time that avian/bat carcasses remain in the search area.  Seven turbine study areas representing the project area’s wide variation in vegetative cover and terrain were randomly selected as a subset of the 36 turbines for each of the nine scavenger trials (Table 2.1).  One chicken carcass representing large birds, two large quail representing medium birds, and two small quail carcasses representing small birds were placed at each of these turbines.  Thirty-five carcasses were distributed at different turbines during each scavenger trial.  Each carcass was dropped from waist height and its location recorded with a GPS unit. Following placement, carcasses were checked each day for the first 4 days and then on days 7, 10, 14, and

## **3.0 Results**

## **3.1 Carcass Searches**

Between July 2007 and December 2008, a total of 18 avian casualties or feather spots and 12 bat carcasses were found at 15 of the 36 study plots.  Avian casualties accounted for 60% of the mortalities, and bat casualties comprised 40% of the mortalities at the study plots.  The carcasses and feather spots consisted of 5 hoary bat ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) carcasses, 4 Mexican free-tailed bat ( _Tadarida brasiliensis_ ) carcasses, 1 hoary or Mexican free-tailed bat, 2 carcasses of an unknown bat species, 5 feather spots of unidentified bird species, 7 turkey vulture ( _Cathartes aura_ ) carcasses and 1 feather spot, 1 ring-necked pheasant ( _Phasianus colchicus_ ) feather spot, 1 unidentified passerine bird carcass, 2 American redstart ( _Steophaga ruticilla_ ) carcasses, and 1 ruby-crowned kinglet ( _Regulus calendula_ ) carcass. The carcasses of 4 turkey vultures, 1 red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ), and 2 hoary bats were found either outside the study area at selected turbines or at turbines that were not part of the study (Table 3.1).

The largest number of carcasses or remains found at any single turbine was 4, at Turbine 167.  Three carcasses were found at each of Turbines 160, 190, and 215, and two carcasses at each of Turbines 120, 132, 146, 158, and 196.  The largest number of carcasses or remains found at any single turbine during any one search was 2 at Turbine 160.  The majority of mortalities occurred during the fall months from August through October with carcasses found during this period comprising about 46% of all recorded fatalities (including fatalities recorded outside study areas).  Approximately 27% of the mortalities occurred in the winter, 19% in the spring and 8% in the summer (Table 3.1).

The distance from the base of the turbines to where avian and bat casualties were found ranged between 2 m (6.6 ft) at Turbine 196 and 146 m (480 ft) at Turbine 167 with an average distance of 39.7 m (130 ft) (Table 3.1). ## **3.1.1 Passerine Birds**

Three of the bird fatalities (13%) found were positively identified as passerines. These included 2 American redstart carcasses and a ruby-crowned kinglet carcass.  In addition, 5 feather spots were found, but could not be identified as to species.  One American redstart was found approximately 33 m (108 ft) south of Turbine 146 during the October 19, 2008 survey. When found the carcass appeared to be about 2 weeks old.

The second American redstart carcass was found roughly 49 m (161 ft) south of Turbine 146 during the November 15, 2008 survey.  The carcass had been scavenged and appeared to have been in place for about 2 weeks.  American redstart are found typically in woodlands and groves (Peterson, 1990) and they have been observed at Buffalo Gap during the fall, however, they are less common in the western part of Texas.  The species migrates to Mexico from August to October and migrate north through west Texas from March through May.

The ruby-crowned kinglet was found approximately 37 m (121 ft) north of Turbine 215 during the October 11, 2008 survey.  It appeared to be a fresh kill (i.e. less than 12 hours old).  Strong winds in the days preceding the survey may have blown this bird off course and into the turbine.  Ruby-crowned kinglets are common residents of Texas during the late fall through the early spring (October through March) (Rappole and Blacklock, 1994).

Finally, an unidentified bird carcass was found near Turbine 132 in December 2008.  The carcass was largely consumed and appeared to be a recent hawk kill rather than a turbine strike.  However, since the possibility of a turbine strike followed by scavenging cannot be ruled out, the carcass was included in our calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.

## **3.1.2 Game Birds**

Game bird mortality comprised about 4% of all avian carcasses or feather spots recorded during this study.  The ring-necked pheasant feather spot was found in a flat grassy area 46 m (151 ft) southwest of Turbine 193 during the May 14, 2008 survey.  The feather spot was comprised of down feathers and lacked primary feathers, indicating that this mortality was probably the result of predator attack rather than a turbine strike.  However, since the possibility of a turbine strike followed by scavenging cannot be ruled out, the carcass was included in calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.

## **3.1.3 Raptors**

Raptor mortalities comprised about 4% of all carcasses or feather spots found during this study.  In late March 2008, the carcass of an adult red-tailed hawk was found along the shoulder of an access road approximately 21 m (69 ft) northeast of Turbine 194.  The carcass appeared to about 2 days old and, though slightly scavenged, was mostly intact.  This bird appeared to have died from a collision with a turbine.  Since the carcass was found outside the survey area, it was not included in the calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.

## **3.1.4 Turkey Vultures**

A total of 12 turkey vulture (52%) carcasses and feather spots were found in this study. The first 3 turkey vulture carcasses were found during the September 2007 survey.  One carcass of an adult was located 2 m (6.6 ft) south of Turbine 213.  The bird was scavenged and appeared to have died within the month.  The second carcass was a juvenile bird and was found in a grassy area, 28 m (92 ft) east of Turbine 190. Another juvenile carcass was found 50 m (164 ft) northwest of Turbine 180.  The vulture appeared to have been scavenged and had been dead for approximately 1 month.  Since the carcass was found outside the survey area, it was not included in the calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.  During the November 15, 2007 survey, another juvenile turkey vulture carcass was found approximately 16 m (52 ft) west of Turbine 83 in a grassy area.  The carcass had been scavenged and appeared to have been struck 4– 8 days previous.  The carcass of a young turkey vulture was found during the April 21, 2008 survey approximately 22 m (72 ft) north of Turbine 157 on an access road near the turbine.  The carcass appeared to be 2 days old.  Since the carcass was found outside the survey area, it was not included in calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.

Three turkey vulture carcasses were found during the survey in the mid-May 2008 survey.  The first, a juvenile bird, was found 35 m (115 ft) north of Turbine 149.  The carcass was scavenged and had been present on-site for approximately 5–7 days.  The second bird also was a juvenile and was found 26 m (85 ft) north of Turbine 157.  The carcass had been heavily scavenged and appeared to have been in the area for 7–10 days.  Since both carcasses were found outside the survey area, they were not included in calculations for estimated facility-related fatalities.  A third carcass consisting of a dismembered wing with primary and some secondary feathers was located 29 m (95 ft) northwest of Turbine 190.  This carcass was estimated to be about 1 month old.

A turkey vulture carcass 35 m (115 ft) northwest of Turbine 120, was found on October 9, 2008.  The carcass was scavenged and appeared to have been present for about 2 weeks.  Another turkey vulture carcass was found near the base of Turbine 120 during the November 2008 survey.

Turkey vultures frequently were observed flying near the turbines.  The adult birds were seen maneuvering around the rotating blades and often circling around the towers or soaring between the rotating turbine blades.  While the birds often are within strike range of the turbine, only one turkey vulture striking the blades was observed during the August 2006 survey at Buffalo Gap 2.

Though the ages of some of the turkey vulture carcasses could not be identified, the majority of those casualties found in September 2007 clearly were juveniles.  Of the 10 turkey vulture carcasses only one was positively identified as a mature adult.  This suggests that the younger birds may not be as facile at maneuvering around the turbines and may be more prone to colliding with the blades than adults.

## **3.1.5 Bats**

Seven hoary bat ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ) carcasses were positively identified during the Buffalo Gap II survey.  The first 3 carcasses were found during the August 16, 2007 survey. The first bat was located 462 m (1515 ft) southwest of Turbine 215 in a juniper area and probably struck the turbine in the previous week.  The second bat was found in a tall stand of grass and junipers, approximately 15 m (49 ft) northwest of Turbine 190.  The carcass was scavenged and the time of death could not be determined.  A third bat was found 231 m (756 ft) north of Turbine 215 on the turbine access road among junipers and sunflowers and had been dead 2–3 days.  Two more bat carcasses were found during the September 2007 survey, with one found 6 m (20 ft) west of Turbine 134.  One carcass appeared to have been in place for less than 5 days.  The other carcass was found in a slightly scavenged condition among junipers and grasses just north of Turbine 215.  Another hoary bat carcass was found during the October 18, 2007 survey approximately 17 m (56 ft) south of Turbine 85.

The carcass was found in a juniper-oak woodland and was estimated to have been present in that location for 1–2 days.  The day before the carcass was found, there had been gusty winds of up to 40 mi per hour. Only one hoary bat carcass was found in 2008.  The carcass was located about 15 m (49 ft) southeast of Turbine 209 and was estimated to be less than 1 week old.

Hoary bats are found throughout the state of Texas and typically migrate south in the winter and northward in the spring.  The species is found in wooded areas such as the juniper-oak woodlands common to the Buffalo Gap II Wind Farm where it roosts from branches or twigs (Davis and Schmidly, 1994).

Four Mexican free-tailed bat ( _Tadarida brasiliensis_ ) carcasses were observed from July 2007 through May 2008.  The first carcass was found during the July 2007, survey in an opening among a juniper-oak stand, 19 m (62 ft) from Turbine 158.  The carcass had been scavenged and appeared to be about 4 days old.  Two carcasses were found during the September 2007, survey, with one found 3 m (10 ft) northwest of Turbine 167.  The carcass was less than 1 week old.  The other bat carcass also was found about 2 m (6.6 ft) east of Turbine 196 in a grassy area.  The carcass had been scavenged and the estimated time since death was 10 days.  A fourth bat carcass was found during the November 15, 2007, survey.  The carcass was found 4 m (13 ft) south of Turbine 177 and was probably less than 8 hours old.  No Mexican free-tailed bat carcasses were observed during the 2008 surveys.

Mexican free-tailed bats are found throughout Texas during the summer, but migrate to Mexico in the fall.  These bats utilize caves, mine tunnels, old wells, human habitations, and bridges where individuals can roost in close association (Nowak 1994).  While no additional field data on habitat use or behavior of bats at Buffalo Gap 2 was collected for this study, observations of bats feeding during the pre-dusk and evening hours in the Buffalo Gap 2 area suggest that the local populations may use the old barns and homesteads that are common to the project area.

In late July, fledglings predominate in the diurnal feeding flights from caves, and they tend to occupy their natal cave until the onset of cool weather in October and November drives them south out of Texas. Mexican free-tailed bats prefer open areas that provide flying insects; however, they also forage in open fields, woodlands, and forested areas (Bat Conservation International 2007).

Three unidentified bat carcasses also were found.  Both were located at Turbine 160 during the July 24, 2007 survey and they may have been from the same cohort.  The first was found 9 m (30 ft) from the turbine and appeared to have been killed 1–3 days prior to the survey.  The second bat was located 39 m (128 ft) west of the turbine and also appeared to have been killed 1–3 days prior to the survey.  The third bat carcass was found during the May 2008 survey.  The carcass had been extensively scavenged and was located 104 m (341 ft) north of Turbine 158.  The approximate age of the carcass was estimated at 6–10 days.

Models were randomly placed at the study turbines from August 2007 through December 2008.  Searcher accuracy also varied among the searchers, and ranged from 6–100% accuracy (Table 3.2). ## **3.2.2 Carcass Removal by Scavengers**

In this phase of the study, a total of 228 mid- sized and small quail carcasses and 57 chicken (large) carcasses were used to determine scavenger removal rates (Appendix C).  The mean length of time (2.07 days) that these three size classes of carcasses remained in the turbine plots prior to being scavenged (residence time) varied by carcass size and by season.  The medium and small quail carcasses remained on-site roughly the same amount of time, with the smaller carcasses averaging 1.64 days and medium carcasses averaging 1.74 days.  The chicken (large) carcasses remained on-site for about half a day longer (2.24 days) than the quail did.  The difference in scavenging time probably is due to the size of these birds and scavenger processing rates, since the bigger carcasses generally take longer to be consumed and are more difficult to carry off.

Schoenfeld’s equation (2004), which is more sensitive to survey interval and searcher accuracy, produced somewhat higher estimates of mortality than that of Erickson et al. (1998) (Table 3.3).  Based on Schoenfeld’s 2004 equation, the estimated number of all facility-related fatalities for the Buffalo Gap II wind project is 19.5 small/medium sized birds, 17.4 (turkey vultures), and 33.5 (bats).

## **4.0 Discussion and Conclusions**

## **4.1 Searcher Accuracy**

Searcher accuracy was estimated at approximately 58% and is somewhat higher than those reported for other wind projects (Erickson et al. 2000, Johnson et al. 2002, Morrison 2002) or when viewed in the context of the dense vegetative cover surrounding the edges of many of the turbine pads.  Although large portions of the turbine study plots were covered with a shrub or tree canopy, the vegetative cover near the ground surface was neither dense nor tall, making it easier to see the ground surface, to find carcasses.

## **4.2 Scavenger Rates**

Carcasses were scavenged the fastest in the summer, with a mean removal time of 1.23 days. Carcass removal periods were longest for carcasses during winter with a mean time of 2.97 days. Mean carcass residence times were consistently higher during the fall (1.67 days) and winter (2.97 days) months than the spring (1.80 days) and summer months (1.23 days).  These rates were similar to those documented in 1991 by Howell and DiDonato, with an approximate loss of 80% of the carcass after 2 days.

A number of scavengers in the immediate area of the Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm that could potentially remove bird carcasses from the study area were observed throughout the study, including feral pigs, raccoons, skunks, armadillos, opossums, coyotes, foxes, various rodents, turkey vultures, and other birds. Some of these animals are able to access the canopies of trees.  This ability was reflected in the observation that several carcasses placed in trees and other vegetation during scavenger trials were removed within days of placement.

A majority of the landowners at Buffalo Gap 2 use their properties for hunting during the fall.  Thus, the low carcass residence time and high scavenging rates documented in this study may be related to the increased availability of carrion or offal at the Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm.  Feral pig carcasses were observed near the Buffalo Gap 2 Wind Farm and likely provided a major food source for turkey vultures and other scavengers in the area. At other wind farms where hunting is not regularly conducted, lower levels of mortality may be spread out across equally large areas and across time with no concentrations of carrion or events that might create a more consistent food resource for the scavengers.

Estimates obtained from this and similar studies are affected by several other sources of bias.  For example, the protocol used to estimate scavenging rates may not take into account how scavengers form “search images” and respond to repeated placement of fresh carcasses in a project area.  This coupled with the availability of offal and carcasses from the fall-winter hunting season probably drew a number of scavengers and other omnivorous animals to the project area.

The use of quail and chicken for these scavenger trials may also have introduced bias to this study in that these birds appear to be scavenged at a higher rate than turkey vultures and other native bird species.  This rapid scavenging rate may have contributed to an underestimation of mean carcass residence time, particularly for turkey vultures.  Observations during the Buffalo Gap 1 study and the on-going Buffalo Gap 3 study indicate that turkey vulture carcass residence times are likely greater than the calculated times for chickens.  Additionally, while most of the intact and scavenged carcasses and feather spots were included in the estimation of the turbine-related fatalities, some of the observed fatalities were undoubtedly caused by factors unrelated to the wind project.  The potential underestimation of mean carcass residence time, as well as the potential for non-turbine related fatalities may have led to an overestimate of the number of fatalities caused by the wind turbines.

## **4.3 Other Factors**

All of the turbines at the Buffalo Gap 2 wind farm are surrounded by or are adjacent to dense vegetation which slowed the surveyors’ efforts to maintain a consistent bearing along the transect route.  However, visual contact of the surfaces for most of the turbine plots could be maintained by the surveyors.  An additional consideration was the possibility of turbine-struck birds becoming entangled or lodged in the dense shrub canopies that rimmed several of the study plots on the edge of the escarpment these birds and/or bats may not have been observed during surveys.  Such casualties would not be readily detected by the surveyors except when plumage or light conditions provide sufficient contrast.  However, carcasses lodged in the canopy may be shaken loose by winds, and may eventually fall to the ground.  The site is very windy, and no-wind days are rare in the project area.

The casualty data in this study indicated most of the species found previously have been observed and recorded at Buffalo Gap 2.  Most of the fatalities (including feather spots) observed in this study occurred during the fall migration period (Table 3.1).

The results of this study suggest that that the monitoring protocol used for this study generally was sufficient to provide data for evaluating the effects of the Buffalo Gap 2 development on larger avian species such as turkey vultures.  The uncertainty associated with assigning a cause of death to feather spots, however, may introduce some uncertainty in the estimates of mortality among the smaller avian species. This uncertainty may have been offset by the size of the plot areas surveyed and the frequency of survey (every 21 days).

This study generally is consistent with the results from the Buffalo Gap I study and the emerging data from the ongoing Buffalo Gap 3 study. The estimates calculated for turkey vultures are especially consistent among the three study phases and may be used to predict future mortality in this species.  There are a number of wind turbine projects that are now operating in the Buffalo Gap area and this study’s results contain information that will be useful in designing future projects, refining the siting or placement of turbines and developing hunting management practices that will avoid contributing to casualties.

## **Appendix E**

**Observations of Resident and Migratory Birds**

All birds species observed within the Buffalo Gap II wind farm during the surveys were recorded.  This list represents an opportunistic sampling rather than a concerted survey effort with a total of 21 different species of birds observed in the project area.  This is not a comprehensive list of all species that may be present or pass through the project area.
